en: Those who are endowed with all virtues and yet free from all faults protect the world on every side.
Salutations always to whomever they may be. || 1 ||
Having understood this, the wise should not allow even the slightest opening for [any action], however small it may be. || 2 ||
This world falls upon virtues and faults according to its very habit,
just as vultures and swans descend [upon their respective prey].
In the case of a cremation ground and a lake, it is so by their very nature.
Generally, in the presence of the wicked,
the excellence of a person attains its fulfillment;
only the *kuruvinda* stone is truly a jewel.
Being pure by birth, it obtains radiance. || 4 ||
Even when mixed with defects [...
one must distinguish the milk from the water.
Who else knows [anything] beyond swans? || 5 ||
Even minute qualities attain great renown when they exist among the virtuous; [just as] the quality of *sīdhu*... // 6 //
In doing harm or benefit to the world, the wicked man and the virtuous man never reach satiety;
for darkness devours the universe.
Savitṛ also always illuminates. || 7 ||
The skill that a wicked person possesses in piercing the vital organs of others is not for a beneficial task; rather,
it is the capacity for causing injury.
That [knowledge] is of no benefit for poison. || 8 ||
Even a virtuous person, like a base man, perceives the faults of others with excessive effort;
however, there is a distinction between these two.
A good person [is able] to drink, while a wicked person is able to speak. || 9 ||
People, greatly tormented by the conduct of the deceitful, remember the virtuous;
they long intensely for the moon.
The world is scorched by the rays of the sun.
Just as a wicked person is intent on creating division among others, so too does a virtuous person strive for reconciliation; yet the needle makes a hole.
Immediately thereafter, the thread covers it.
Even virtues as pure as moonbeams become faults in the presence of the wicked;
even gold becomes [like] rumā-salt in the desert.
Once it has fallen, it simply becomes ash. || 12 ||
Upon seeing the suffering of another,
only a base person feels joy, not one of noble birth; for generally, [the brave] quiver in battle.
The weapons are indeed made of iron.
The wicked know only how to revile the virtuous, whereas the good know how to praise them;
the cold season withers the lotus, yet it causes the jasmine to bloom.
Only spring causes the forest to blossom. || 14 ||
For in the Kali age, even among great beings, there are generally those who are harmful, lacking in sharp discernment, and of a cruel and stubborn nature due to their violent disposition.
Only those who are ruthless are fit [for this]. || 15 ||
The virtuous person abandons even the slightest evil, whereas the non-virtuous person does not abandon even a great one;
yet the hand touches even the flame of fire.
But the eye cannot endure even a speck of dust. || 16 ||
Even when a wise person speaks what is beneficial,
the mind of the deceitful does not find clarity;
for a jewel arises only from a source of jewels.
When the cloud thunders, it arises. || 17 ||
Even when treated with excessive honor, a base person does not lead to one's welfare;
he merely soils one's head.
The impure dust has been cast far away. || 18 ||
Like a crest-jewel endowed with excellent qualities, even when worn upon the head, it adorns a man;
so too does saffron, even when applied only to the surface.
It illuminates the sandalwood indeed. || 19 ||
Through reasoning, one produces a conception of the world that corresponds exactly to its true nature;
however, excessive elaboration does not shine.
Like hair and nails, so are the wicked. || 20 ||
That the acute accent rises high and the grave accent falls low is appropriate;
yet the moonlight falls upon the ground.
The darkness takes refuge in the cavities. || 21 ||
One who is exalted by noble lineage overcomes even the most haughty of the wicked, even if struck down a hundred times;
those of inferior birth do not shine.
Even the bright sun [is surpassed] by the gem born before it. || 22 ||
The fame of one who possesses virtues alone radiates through the ten directions, obstructing the renown of his enemies; it does not shine in the mirror of one who is deformed.
A beautiful reflection arises. || 23 ||
The receding of the ocean, the setting of the sun, the waning of the moon, and the fall of the virtuous— these are all transitory.
They never deviate from increase. || 24 ||
Lifespans, the youthfulness of the young, the flames of fire, the currents of rivers, and the heights of the wicked— [all these are transient].
Once gone, they do not return again. || 25 ||
Due to an attachment to unaccustomed qualities, the wicked man finds no stability in a pure position;
like a bee that abandons sandalwood.
They dissolve only into corpses. || 26 ||
Even when treated with extreme courtesy, the deceitful never abandon their innate nature,
even by Maheśvara himself bowing his head.
Is it not the case that the moon itself has been held crooked? || 27 ||
Even a fault is dear to the world when it belongs to great souls, like the bristling of hair on elephants;
but in the case of a wicked person, it is like that of a bow.
Even a virtue may lead to the harm of the world. || 28 ||
Like the wind,
these common people generally take on the form of others through association; but the virtuous are like the rays of the sun.
Even in the conjunction of the existent and the non-existent, they remain unattached. || 29 ||
One who has desisted from harming others and possesses good character brings delight even without conscious intent;
for even a rainbow, though devoid of inherent qualities, brings joy.
For the adornment of heaven and earth. || 30 ||
Where is the base person, and where is greatness?
Where are the noble and virtuous, and where is calamity?
In the separation of like things, there is a dullness of heart.
Whom does this element not torment? || 31 ||
Even that which is lowly, when embraced by great souls, attains supreme greatness;
even a crystal stone becomes red [when touched by a red object].
Through wholesome deeds, one attains a ruby. || 32 ||
In the world, people [are known] by their conduct alone;
it is their very enjoyment that reveals [them].
The quality of good fortune belonging to a playful woman. || 33 ||
Some speak but do nothing; others accomplish their task even without being told. Even a flowerless arrow bears fruit.
The milky tree, however, bears fruit even without flowering.
For a living being, mere virtue is not enough to prevent crookedness, nor is mere vice sufficient to ensure it;
for even a straight arrow kills.
Even when crooked, the fruit protects its own body. || 35 ||
Better is one who is very sharp yet straightforward than a mild fire of chaff covered by the grass of deceit;
for even from the heat of a cloudless summer sun, [the former provides relief].
The morning sun burns even more intensely than the noonday heat.
Through association with the wise, even the dull-witted become conversant with the conduct of the clever;
this is taught by women who are full of passion.
The graceful charms belong to the intoxication of youth alone.
From the very beginning, those of poor wisdom corrupt their minds even toward their teachers;
it is said that fish must be killed.
Thus do the fishermen sow hemp. || 38 ||
That "this one has a peaceful form, so no danger arises from him" is not an absolute certainty;
for white [substances] may become collyrium, and black [substances] likewise.
Do lamps not produce flames? || 39 ||
Even this uncertainty— "this one is terrible in appearance, there is danger from him"—
becomes a source of great terror.
The form of Śiva is for the sake of Śiva alone. || 40 ||
It is reasonable that those who are frivolous should consider recklessness to be a virtue; it is observed even among the seeds of the *guñjā* plant.
The Pulindas have coral-colored [garments]. || 41 ||
Even virtues, through long familiarity, cause beings to turn their backs;
just as those who are extremely thirsty [turn away] from water.
While drinking, they indeed become estranged. || 42 ||
Even when applied, those who lack skillful means do not accomplish their tasks;
straight arrows, too, [miss] the target.
They do not go [there] because of their perverted intentions. || 43 ||
Occupying a high position,
people generally become deluded regarding the true nature of things;
they perceive even the uneven as level.
He ascended to the very peak of the mountain summit. || 44 ||
This is some kind of sorcery, since even when the basis is equally slight,
the transactions and the words differ.
They do not meet, just as the faces of men [do not meet]. || 45 ||
Even when gratified by virtues,
subjects do not bow without the use of force; even though it rests upon its own body, the lute does not sound without being struck.
It is said that she sounds sweetly even when not struck. || 46 ||
The association of the great with the base finds no union, just as gold does not unite with iron;
the lute does not blend its sound with the drum.
She was virtuous and possessed a beautiful voice. || 47 ||
Only when those possessing virtues associate with other virtuous people does their union become pure, enduring, and free from decay;
the fragrance wafts for a very long time.
[The flowers] are found only on the *kakubha* and other such trees. || 48 ||
The virtuous generally do not abandon one who has taken refuge in them, even if that person lacks merit,
provided they have remained devoted and shared in both their growth and decline.
The moon bears even its own spot.
The power of the strong is manifested only in times of adversity, not in prosperity;
likewise, there is no fragrance in agallochum when it is not burning.
It exists previously, just as in the case of that which has fallen into fire.
Even a very small measure of the wealth of the virtuous is to be enjoyed by the great, whereas even the entire earth is not the fortune of the wicked;
for water is refreshing only when it possesses essence.
She does not remove [the heat] from the Lord of the Sea. || 51 ||
Just as faults appear large when [the moon] is great, they do not appear so even when slightly diminished;
this is observed in the full moon.
As there is a stain [in the moon], so it is not in the child. || 52 ||
Though destitute of power, the ignoble man incites the world toward malice;
he sharpens the edge of his sword.
A stone is itself incapable of cutting. || 53 ||
A person is sharp-sighted regarding the offense of another even when it is distant, yet not so regarding his own even when it is close at hand; he does not see his own wound in his eye.
He points out the spot on the moon. || 54 ||
Even a wise person does not shine when set upon a wrong path due to contradiction;
even a lute with all its strings is but a mere sound to a listener [who lacks appreciation].
A stringless lute does not produce sound. || 55 ||
Even one born dull-witted is not able to accomplish in a moment that which a wise man accomplishes; for even a form acquired over an eon [is surpassed by him].
Does the eye not see even a horse? || 56 ||
The powerful strike down everything loftily, not that which is naturally humble;
for the thunderbolt generally falls upon what is already low.
Only on the mountain peaks, and not upon the grass. || 57 ||
Only when weak does one display power through the horn of speech;
only when blunted does one strike against a stone.
The crucible emits an excess of heat. || 58 ||
Even today, many— even those who are skillful— do not reach the end of the conduct of rogues,
for the sake of the tears of a courtesan.
Even the veteran libertines do not know this. || 59 ||
Free from passion, highly precious, flawless, most steadfast, and gentle toward those who cause division—
she is like the crest-jewel of the virtuous.
Even the slightest association does not waver.
Fleeting, light by nature,
difficult to manage, fragile, and harsh in its essence—
association with the base causes such torment.
Like a flame of fire, even though it has grown exceedingly great. || 61 ||
"Tell me of association with the wicked: at first it causes shame,
in the middle it brings humiliation, and at the end it is bitter."
If there is anything at all that is well-established, [then... 62.
Fellow practitioners of the holy life generally perceive the virtue of the world,
even its most subtle movement within the water.
A fish knows the [intention] of a fish. || 63 ||
The seed of assistance, when sown in good soil, does not sprout in the salty wasteland; even a tiny drop of oil [spreads].
It blooms in water, not upon sands.
Causing distress, harsh, acting recklessly, and fearful—
she is like a wife devoid of truth.
Speech destroys a man before long. || 65 ||
The wise strike at the roots of their enemies, while the unskilled strike at the branches; a dog becomes enraged at a clod of earth.
But the king of beasts is hostile toward the man. || 66 ||
The fires of enemies are extinguished by the very water of virtue, not by the grass of faults;
for it is light alone that dispels darkness.
Darkness is never at all to be avoided. || 67 ||
Anger first devours the angry man himself, and it does not stop at others; fire necessarily consumes its own source as well.
But it does not necessarily burn anything other than that. || 68 ||
Even an unskilled person travels safely by following the very path made by the wise;
such is the power of the diamond.
The thread enters into the center of the gem. || 69 ||
Whatever purpose an ignorant person accomplishes, that for him is "like the crow and the palm fruit" (accidental);
it is achieved by fate in some way or another through the syllable [of destiny].
Even the wood-boring insect bores into pieces of wood. || 70 ||
Not all who study necessarily obtain the fruit of their knowledge;
it is like a camel that constantly carries saffron.
Because it flows away, one does not touch it. || 71 ||
By their very nature, the virtuous generally meet with destruction among the ignoble;
parrots, for instance, are merely those who speak clearly.
They are bound in a cage. || 72 ||
Even an enemy who is easily subdued becomes difficult to overcome when he has taken refuge with one of great power;
even the sun is not able to consume him.
Like a drop of water poured into the ocean. || 73 ||
It either goes to the very limit or does not begin at all; it is great and remains uninitiated.
Wherever it falls, it causes a split.
Or else, a great thunderbolt does not fall at all. || 74 ||
An ignorant person is not capable of discerning the distinction between virtues and faults, even when that distinction is easy to perceive,
just like a creature whose eyes have been stolen away.
Light and darkness become equal. || 75 ||
Even one who has desisted from evil, if he is deceitful, will inevitably act wickedly when encountering the right conditions,
just as wood that remains charred will eventually ignite even after a long time.
Sprinkled with nectar-water, it vomits fire. || 76 ||
In the rise of a friend, one who is pale, whose sole defect is revealed, and whose essence is excessive,
finds no satisfaction through the depletion of his affection.
The wicked person approaches [the virtuous] like a lamp. || 77 ||
When there is an audience, the words of eloquent speakers shine forth without obstacle in the assembly,
just as barley [thrives] only upon reaching the earth.
It attains purity like a gem from stone;
an object fallen into both the good and the bad equally becomes a vessel for praise and blame.
Poison in the mouth of a serpent, or even water, becomes a pearl within an oyster shell. || 79 ||
I am the leader, the most excellent in the assembly of kings, and everywhere in the city;
I alone am his friend.
Skilled in ethics and proficient in poetry. || 80 ||
Thus, the ignorant themselves proclaim their own broken dignity through bold words, ignoble speech, and harsh actions.
The poverty of the wealth of learning lies within. 81.
One who possesses only the strength of meager learning generally displays his verbal prowess loudly;
for everywhere, it is indeed the bad actor who does so.
The drama mocks [the world] excessively. || 82 ||
One who is intent on what is impossible is generally a fool, not a wise man;
for who other than a child would [seek to drink] from water?
Desiring to seize the shimmering orb of the moon. || 83 ||
A wise person should not employ those possessed of good qualities in menial tasks;
for those capable of bearing every burden are [lost] among the wicked.
Great bulls are not yoked to a tethering rope. || 84 ||
A person of weak character undergoes extreme transformation even from a slight cause of offense,
just as a small tree trembles even in a gentle breeze.
The king alone rises very high. || 85 ||
Only the wicked, having seized the yoke before them, drag those possessed of virtues forward;
[just as] only wood and straw [are used] for the ocean's [bridges].
Jewels do not float upon the surface. || 86 ||
The mind delights in the greatness of the great alone, not in that of a lowly atom;
clarified butter stays upon water.
The honey flows down by itself. || 87 ||
If it were dullness, if it were brilliance—
then everything would be merely dull, not wise;
for a stone sinks in water.
When struck, it vomits fire. || 88 ||
A wicked person, once brought near, serves only to cause injury,
unless he is used to slaughter another.
What else can be accomplished by a treatise? || 89 ||
Some are skilled only in explaining the treatise, while others are capable of applying it;
the hand, however, brings the food to one's mouth.
But the tongue alone perceives tastes. || 90 ||
Out of delusion, people generally sink in water that is difficult to cross, even when it reaches only their knees;
the wise, however, [cross] by the power of skillful means.
They turn even the ocean into a cow's footprint. || 91 ||
The wise are able to restrain themselves from calamities, whereas those of little strength cannot; it is like śarabhas [restraining] themselves by their very breaths.
They draw water from a well. || 92 ||
That lightness of mind by which even insignificant riches intoxicate,
even as the webs of spiders do.
The fly and the mosquito meet their end. || 93 ||
The multitude of sense objects brings a base person under its control, but not a noble person;
for it binds only the gnat.
A spider's web cannot hold an elephant.
Even those who are insignificant attain the status of the virtuous by attending upon one who possesses excellence,
just as small plants on the peaks of the Snowy Mountains.
But even snows become like frost. || 95 ||
Even a single speck of dust, when spoken of, obscures hundreds of virtues;
it is like the mark on the moon that one seeks to wipe away.
Even many virtues are not able [to overcome it]. || 96 ||
Only the virtuous are capable of rescuing one in calamity, not the serpents that are the wicked;
they alone enable the world to cross over the waters.
A boat itself causes a stone to sink. || 97 ||
Even at a distance, the good and the wicked feel joy and displeasure respectively upon the rise of one possessed of virtues;
for the lotus blossoms when the sun rises.
The night-lotuses wither when the sun is present. || 98 ||
That the wicked delight in faults rather than virtues is not surprising;
they wear the feathers of peacocks.
Even having abandoned their jewels, the Pulindas [fled]. || 99 ||
Greedy for the flesh on the backs of others, crawling about as soon as it obtains some slight pleasure, the mind of the wicked is like a female snake.
It constantly falls upon wounds alone. || 100 ||
Those who delight in virtues do not grieve even upon seeing a fault in a person endowed with merit; just as one does not feel distress when seeing a spot fallen upon the moon out of affection for it.
The world perceives even a flaw. || 101 ||
Even when relying on a perfectly pure livelihood, a wicked person causes distress to others;
even serpents that subsist only on air are venomous.
They do not abandon harming others. || 102 ||
Having attributed faults even to the virtuous, the wicked afflict the world;
they do so even by fashioning a wheel in the sky.
Spiders kill mosquitoes. || 103 ||
For one whose mind is afflicted by the poison of sense-objects,
what indeed is there that a wicked person will not do?
Even a bone, though foul-smelling and tasteless, [is consumed].
Does a dog, tormented by hunger, not lick it? || 104 ||
The wicked reveal their own true nature most cruelly toward the virtuous;
tigers kill deer.
But even when dead, they do not take up the lion. || 105 ||
Whether straight, crooked, young, or old, the moon always takes [the life] away;
there is never a state in which that does not occur.
Where a good person does not do what is pleasing [to others]. || 106 ||
The world speaks falsely when it says that enmity arises solely from a cause;
what indeed could be the purpose of such a claim?
The snake and the mongoose are always enemies.
The ignoble person constantly and excessively oppresses even the virtuous man who remains unchanged;
what harm has been done by the lotus plant?
That which always burns away the cold. || 108 ||
Even when capable of retaliation, virtuous persons do not act harmfully;
they endure even violent assaults.
The earth does not equal the sky. || 109 ||
Ignorant of doing no harm, yet constantly skilled in the misfortunes of the entire world—
this is some kind of unchaste nature.
For the sake of tormenting others, indeed, is the conduct of the wicked. || 110 ||
Even upon hearing [of their success], the base suffer great distress; what talk can there be of their prosperity?
Even when the sun has risen, a lamp does not shine.
Does it shine, or rather, is it midday? || 111 ||
The wise are unable to speak of the faults of others, even when they exist, just as they are unable to speak of their own virtues.
[They refrain from speaking] of the faults of others just as they do of their own virtues.
Indeed, villains speak even of that which does not exist. || 112 ||
A virtuous person feels shame even when reproached by another, whereas a wicked person feels no shame at all for failing to do what ought to be done.
"Alas for this meanness, that she should vomit it up herself! || 113 ||
Only the wicked are capable of subduing the wicked, never a virtuous person; [just as] the medicine for the disease of leprosy [is derived from the same source].
They desire a suitable, unharmed tree.
Even those possessed of virtues are first of all oppressed by rogues who are exceedingly arrogant;
for Fortune resides upon the breasts of women.
Thus, among these, old age falls first. || 115 ||
Those who are already beset by calamities listen to the words of evil friends when their misfortunes have arisen.
Indifference alone tastes most sweet. || 116 ||
For the world, which abounds in suffering, joy is fragile and calamity is great;
childhood and old age endure for a very long time.
But youth lasts for only a few days. || 117 ||
For those who have a purpose, mere courtesy is sufficient and not required in every case; indeed, it is usually just politeness.
In some cases, there is devotion to the reality of women. || 118 ||
Both of these are ill-placed: meanness in the wise and zeal for the dull-witted;
wickedness does not shine upon the head.
Even hair does not look beautiful on the face. || 119 ||
A wise person overcomes even those who are haughty and dull-witted, despite being devoid of wealth;
just as divine water, though falling down, [surpasses] [the heights].
It pacifies the dust that is about to rise up. || 120 ||
He who approaches others relying on the intoxication of thinking "I am strong" is not a wise man;
even for the sun, during its southern course—
The brilliance of one who has departed becomes dull. || 121 ||
Even when fallen into distress, the wise do not enjoy prosperity that is mixed with humiliation;
they do not drink water from the earth.
The phrase "along with pollen" refers specifically to the *cātaka* birds. 122.
The world itself generally teaches even a person of virtuous character crooked ways;
it only spreads more fuel for the fire.
The power to burn belongs to that which consumes the oblation. || 123 ||
The mind of the great alone remains the same in both extreme elevation and downfall;
it is as unchanging as that of the sun.
The mandala [is present] at both sunrise and sunset. || 124 ||
The moon, being mild, is indeed able to endure the daily suffering of waning; however,
the sharp one inevitably sets.
But it does not tolerate being broken, like the sun. || 125 ||
A person does not abandon a dear and devoted person when they are healthy, but rather during times of misfortune; such is the condition that prevails when one falls into calamity.
He is even prepared to give up his life. || 126 ||
Companions exist only so long as a living being has not encountered hardship;
when the thunderbolt falls upon the head, they are gone.
Who is able to protect whom? || 127 ||
Those who experience the state of being assailed by enemies do not perceive it when they are at ease; nor do they perceive the fluctuation of the stream.
Being carried along, he discerns. || 128 ||
Without the friction of the base, those situated within do not attain supreme stability; it is only in fire that gold [reaches its perfection].
Being purified, it attains auspiciousness. || 129 ||
How can one who possesses virtues but does not act for the benefit of others be distinguished from one devoid of virtues?
He is no different from one who has set.
Even when risen, that which does not illuminate [is not the sun]. || 130 ||
People do not recognize the excellence of their own virtues until the fruit has been produced;
such is the power of mantras.
He perceives himself as subduing serpents. || 131 ||
Someone may be powerful in a certain respect,
yet no single individual is sufficient to accomplish all goals;
the thunderbolt shatters the mountain.
It goes by itself to its destruction by means of its own horn. || 132 ||
Due to the difficulty of purifying one's innate nature, there are some among the noble-born who are exceedingly fierce,
even though they have emerged from cool waters.
The lotuses bloom because of the heat. || 133 ||
Even one with strong wings, desiring to kill and having gone very far by means of a throw,
every such agent falls down of his own accord.
Like an arrow whose momentum has been exhausted. || 134 ||
Objects once attained and then lost cause the heart even greater longing,
like those seen for a moment in a dream.
They are deprived of the embrace of their beloveds, who are so difficult to find.
Though they have attained them, these wretched ones, due to their own past actions, are unable to enjoy the pleasures;
it is said that their mouths become inflamed.
For when the grapes have ripened, [there is] indeed [the eating] of the crows. || 136 ||
Even with a very slight rise,
the wicked generally become all-devouring; yet the ocean, even by the waters of the entire world, remains as it was.
It never transgresses its boundary. || 137 ||
The years of a eunuch pass away constantly through two ways alone, like those of a hunter who excessively oppresses others.
Or for one who is being oppressed by another. || 138 ||
Even by seeing a person but once, the wise weigh their worthiness and worthlessness;
for the skilled can do so even by the touch of their hand.
They understand the measure of a pala. || 139 ||
They digest poison, they seize serpents, they even strike down thunderbolts,
and they subdue even the elephants of the quarters.
What indeed is impossible for those who are skillful? || 140 ||
The mind is purified through suffering,
yet it sinks into evils by its very nature;
it becomes defiled of its own accord.
One should wear white clothing with great care. || 141 ||
For even when an enemy possesses little wealth but is guided by policy, the wise exert greater effort;
it is like [the effort required] when there is only a very small amount of water.
Boats are steered with effort. || 142 ||
Even those who lack affection teach devotion for the sake of profit;
like courtesans, they delight people.
And they do not become attached through their disposition. || 143 ||
Disease, that which is born from an egg, a sprout, fire, poison, a mule, woodworms, and parasites in a wound— these,
as well as men who are ungrateful by nature, [perish].
They increase without destroying their own substratum. || 144 ||
Excessive fortune does not reside in those possessed of virtues,
for even the wealthy are generally destitute of virtue; yet the karṇikāra flower is exceedingly beautiful.
The fragrant flowers of the clove tree. || 145 ||
Exceedingly fickle, unstable in its qualities, difficult to grasp, and unsubmissive, it is filled with defects—
just as the taste of the virtuous is [attained] through yoga.
Without having bound the mind, how can there be prosperity? || 146 ||
Do not yield to pride in prosperity,
nor fall into despair in times of misfortune;
for even darkness, once dispelled, may rise again.
Even the risen sun goes to its setting. || 147 ||
Leaving behind even the very great and stable mountain ranges of their lineage due to the fault of pride,
rivers flow toward the ocean.
Behold the greatness of being free from pride! || 148 ||
It is not appropriate to place trust in one of wicked nature simply because he is well-born and virtuous; for is it not said that even sandalwood from the Malaya mountains [can be tainted]?
A fire that has been kindled certainly burns. || 149 ||
Even by a slight [fault], the virtuous, who are naturally delicate, experience agitation,
just as upon seeing food that is poisonous.
The eyes of the cakora bird are flowing [with tears]. || 150 ||
Due to their innate wickedness,
even the virtues of the unrighteous cause distress to the world,
just like the scent of poisonous flowers.
Even a fragrant scent bewilders the minds. || 151 ||
For a lowly person who has attained high status overcomes his master first;
dust rising upward first strikes the feet.
One restrains only that which causes one to arise. || 152 ||
That which is held upon the heads of the great,
that very thing the lowly regard as mere straw;
yet the wise bow to the emblem [of the deity].
But the crow makes it his seat. || 153 ||
By that very same means by which the dull-witted sink, the wise cross over difficulties;
iron, when formed into a solid mass, sinks in water.
That very thing, when made into a vessel, floats. || 154 ||
Health for those who cause harm, wealth for the miserly, power for the ignorant,
and long life for those who eat the strength of others.
Only for the sake of injury, not for greatness. || 155 ||
Whether they are righteous or deceitful,
kings are generally a source of torment; yet, regarding the burning [of the body], they are no more than the fire of the funeral pyre.
And there is a specific rule regarding the Āhavanīya fire. || 156 ||
Those who desire victory do not submit unless they have been overcome; this is the nature of things,
just as objects heated by fire bend.
Metals join metals. || 157 ||
Out of compassion for all living beings, even the radiant and noble bow down on earth for the welfare of the world, just as the sun does.
The hands fall even when they have reached a high position. || 158 ||
Generally, it is only the vulgar who flare up excessively toward those who are mild, not the virtuous man;
oil spreads upon water.
Spit ghee congeals.
Even when extremely provoked, virtuous people become mild through spiritual practice, but not the weak;
for even gold, though hard, [becomes pliable through fire].
There is no means for grass to flow. || 160 ||
Even while assisting them, a base person harms the virtuous; how much more so when striking them?
What need is there even to mention malice?
Even the laughter of Yama brings death. || 161 ||
Virtues seek out the possessor of virtues of their own accord, just as faults seek out the wicked man through devotion;
who would ever poison a precious gem?
Or it lightens even pieces of cotton from the *kāśa* grass. || 162 ||
Even when powerful through wealth and learning,
a wicked person does not abandon his habit of harming others; like a jewel set in an ornate casket, he remains dangerous even when surrounded by beauty.
Does a rhinoceros abandon its habit of harming others? || 163 ||
Even among beings who are exceedingly numerous, those qualities are rare in which they exist; and those lands on earth where they are found are few.
From which jewels are born. || 164 ||
The wise take up only the virtues from those who possess faults, setting aside the defects,
just as bees take nectar even from poisonous flowers.
They drink only honey, not bitterness. || 165 ||
Like threads joined together, even men who are weak become difficult to sever when united;
they can even obscure the sun.
Even the locusts flew up simultaneously. || 166 ||
Even servants who are equal and well-disposed may become harmful to kings, just as wholesome food, when consumed in equal measure, can be detrimental.
Clarified butter and honey become poison. || 167 ||
Even those of poor intelligence generally study knowledge for the sake of humiliating others; such,
it is said, was Yamaghaṇṭā among the worlds.
It resounds incessantly only to inspire terror. || 168 ||
Even from the worthless one may come a man of virtue, and from the virtuous may arise those of wicked conduct;
from the mud rises the lotus.
Even from a lotus, worms arise. || 169 ||
That which is hollow indeed becomes as deep as a dilapidated well due to its smallness;
the ocean, however, is exceedingly shallow.
Although unfathomable due to the greatness of its primordial nature, || 170 ||
When the king is preoccupied with external affairs, noble qualities, like virtues, do not attain their highest excellence; it is as if one were dwelling in houses infested with venomous serpents.
It is not good that lamps shine [in this manner]. || 171 ||
Those who are not great-souled do not know how to honor those who have fallen into misfortune;
[they do not honor] one whose head has only its top-knot remaining.
Hara bears the moon. || 172 ||
Even sages do not bestow their favor upon one who stands at their feet but behaves deceitfully,
like a person suffering from nasal catarrh and a cold fever.
What is the use of sandalwood paste? || 173 ||
Even upon hearing of the virtues of an enemy, the fact that a virtuous person feels an inner throbbing joy even while concealing it reveals their affection for him.
With tears and the emergence of horripilation. || 174 ||
Doing good to those who do harm,
compassion even toward the great, lack of agitation in times of hardship, and the desire to give when in adversity.
These are the signs of exalted greatness. || 175 ||
Even sour speech that is well-spoken destroys burning pain and constipation, like *āranāla*; however,
the speech of a rogue is like the *badara* fruit.
It causes division even among people who are sweet-natured. || 176 ||
To benefit others without seeking recognition, to forgive those who are inferior without being asked, to give unasked, and to win others over through virtuous qualities.
Among hundreds, only a few truly understand. || 177 ||
It is possible to know much and to accomplish what is difficult through action,
as far as the eye can see.
To that extent, the sense of touch does not touch its object. || 178 ||
Even from a person destitute of wealth, one who is poor in spirit suffers, remaining unhappy despite being always rich,
due to inner distress in the heat of summer.
The elephants suffer all the more. || 179 ||
The light are capable of light tasks, while the heavy alone are able to perform weighty duties;
frost destroys the dust.
The arrival of the clouds refreshes the earth. || 180 ||
Through the very passion for giving, the great attain perfection in virtue;
they are not overcome by attachment itself.
Mango trees attain the state of being *sahakāra* (cooperators). || 181 ||
In this world of manifold splendor, nothing is dear to everyone;
the lotus yearns for the sun.
But the moon is pleasing to the night-lily. || 182 ||
Even when purified by wholesome qualities, those who are turbid become disenchanted in an instant;
even copper, though polished, [may turn back to its original state].
For it is once again enveloped by impurity. || 183 ||
The injury done by another finds no long-lasting place within the minds of great-souled ones,
just as a corpse does not remain for even a single night.
He does not dwell together with the ocean. || 184 ||
Though being mocked and deceived by sophists, the world does not realize it; it is enticed by songs as if by hunters.
Even today, deer are being slaughtered. || 185 ||
He alone who is capable of restraint is capable of bestowing grace;
he both withers and gives.
Only the sun [dries] the waters, not the moon. || 186 ||
What is the use of one who, like a child, does not perceive reality— even if he is learned? Both of these are equally blind.
One whose eyes are distorted and one whose eyes are not serene. || 187 ||
Those who are learned say that application to the scriptures without fruit is a vice;
it merely quenches thirst without providing true utility.
One does not overcome diseases by the collection of elixirs.
Between one who is unlearned, great,
and naturally light-minded, and one who is learned, the former is better;
for it is the axe that fells the forests.
A sharp razor is powerful among the hairs. || 189 ||
Aside from causing distress, what else can a base person do even to a friend? [He acts] like one who,
out of fear of the impure poison of a corpse, [flees].
What is the nature of this other odor? || 190 ||
Even when undergoing great suffering, wicked people do not abandon their intent to harm others;
fire may indeed be extinguished.
But it does not abandon its own inherent heat. || 191 ||
In one whose inner self is conquered by vices,
discourses on discipline find no place at all,
just as [dye] on cloth already stained with indigo.
The dye of saffron is difficult to remove. || 192 ||
The humble are said to be wretched,
while the arrogant are said to be proud; the middle course is better,
for it is the balance that attains the status of a standard of authority.
And [he abandons] both pride and humiliation. || 193 ||
Generally, those of a base nature do not become beneficial unless they have been humbled;
the aśoka tree blooms most profusely when trodden upon.
By the blow of the courtesan's feet. || 194 ||
Everyone, even one who acts for the benefit of others, necessarily causes pain to another; yet,
by taking [wealth] away, he brings joy to the world.
The moon alone is the dispeller of the fear of darkness. || 195 ||
Even when a queen is gracious,
the confidence of her attendants does not endure;
those intoxicated by drink harbor suspicion.
They produce [it] even while offering salutations. || 196 ||
Because of the delicacy of their nature,
the virtuous rejoice even at the prosperity of others;
it is like the cleaning of one's nails.
The eyes become exceedingly clear. || 197 ||
Whatever one may perceive to be good in any place, even if it belongs to someone who is not virtuous, one should take that from them; for such things may be found anywhere, even in the Kali age.
Jewels and virtues are born. || 198 ||
From the lion, the king of beasts, the hunter, the boar, the cuckoo, the peacock, the water-dog, the elephant,
the horse, the mule, the donkey, and the camel—
And one should learn from the wives of gamblers. || 199 ||
All these accounts must be understood by those who wish to follow the ways of the world; they are the vital secrets of the Śākinīs.
One who does not know the proper occasion does not understand. || 200 ||
Even when instructed, the deceitful do not abandon their own views due to their crookedness;
even when cut down, a bamboo thicket grows back.
It is difficult to draw out from the middle of a bamboo stalk. || 201 ||
The prosperity of the wicked is like a mirage; the learning of the unrighteous is like flowers on a vidula tree;
and the wealth of the miserly is likewise.
With what in view were they created by the Ordainer? || 202 ||
Only two perform the welfare of others without hesitation, even amidst their own suffering:
he who is exceedingly dull-witted, like an ox, and [the bodhisattva].
Or one who has reached the further shore of awakening. || 203 ||
In this world, both fools and those of pure intellect are constantly intent on helping others;
however, this much is the difference between them.
One [acts] out of delusion, the other out of compassion. || 204 ||
Even if, among hundreds, there should be some single person who does not benefit from reasoning, even in that case, for those of inferior intellect—
The desire to speak of faults is extreme villainy. (205)
Only two in the world are happy, and only two maintain their dignity with composure:
either one who has desisted from all desires, or...
Or one who possesses all that is desirable. || 206 ||
The faults remain powerful only so long as these are not properly applied;
for those who are discouraged despite being engaged in practice.
O wise ones, do not fear the afflictions. || 207 ||
The stone of the latent tendencies of the afflictions, heated in the fire of wisdom and cast into the water of meditative concentration,
is shattered into a hundred pieces.
Like a sugar-crystal stone cast into water. || 208 ||
Though they are capable, they do not venture to accomplish what is to be accomplished when they are thwarted by things that cannot be accomplished;
it is like a sword blunted against a stone.
One should even cut down a plantain tree with effort. || 209 ||
Pure in his lineage and endowed with virtue,
the good man is drawn forth easily like a bow;
yet he may perish at will even when not at the proper time.
A wicked person is like a pestle; he does not bend. || 210 ||
Where that which is to be accomplished is achieved by wisdom alone, there is no role for treatises in the heat of battle, hair-to-hair.
Arrows become fruitless and insignificant. || 211 ||
Whatever is most easily accomplished by a particular means, that alone should be employed for it;
for arrows are capable of piercing through distinctions.
But upon cutting [the roots], the intentions are bound. || 212 ||
A wicked person destroys at a single stroke the virtuous conduct of the great, even if it has been accumulated over an eon;
water, however, increases the grain.
The fire burns gradually, yet in an instant [it consumes everything]. || 213 ||
The fickle reach their highest state among the dull-witted, but never among the great; the stars shine only in dense darkness.
They do not shine before Pūṣan. || 214 ||
The mind, naturally pure,
finds tranquility even within the inner apartments of the meritorious; it is not so for tigers.
They establish peaceful forest retreats. || 215 ||
"This world speaks the truth when it says that those who have shown affection for the wicked perish;
living beings proceed with safety only [when dealing with the good]."
For some, they are like playing with venomous snakes. || 216 ||
Even the Vinaya does not surpass wicked people by means of purity of intention; even with saffron robes, one cannot deceive deer.
Hunters kill after having gained their trust. || 217 ||
At first, everywhere, the deceitful praise only their own brilliance for the sake of gaining influence;
it may turn out to be either gold or iron.
Only through heat does it become workable. || 218 ||
When the minister possesses pure intelligence, the king's power remains unimpeded;
it is like the power of sight when the eye is clear on the path.
The steps of those who walk do not falter. || 219 ||
This is not a matter for contempt—
that the powerful are not pleased with those possessed of virtue; it is like the case of pearls before the learned.
What weight can there be for one whose eyes have departed? || 220 ||
The wealthy man bestows wealth upon the seeker;
the seeker [bestows] merit and fame upon the wealthy man;
yet even so, it is the wealthy man who possesses honor.
The teacher does not go seeking wealth; rather, it is the seeker who approaches him.
The speech of honey flows from the mouths of the crafty; their dealings proceed beyond the edge of a razor.
Their conduct toward serpents and the like is of another sort.
The cry of another is that of a peacock. || 222 ||
Expedients succeed through the power of a sovereign and his minister;
even a firm blow cuts through what is solid.
By means of the binding of the fist and the sword. || 223 ||
Even those who have achieved mastery in the scriptures stumble in their duty when struck by fate;
a blind man does not see the path.
Even by means of a lamp placed in the hand. || 224 ||
One should associate with those who are firm in dharma and artha during times of adversity, but who are inclined toward pleasure in times of well-being;
for life is dependent upon food.
The fruit of body-unguents is play. || 225 ||
Excessive partiality toward anything is neither for one's welfare nor is it hatred;
[likewise is] the consumption of food of a single flavor.
Physicians do not speak for the sake of strength. || 226 ||
The wise praise impartiality alone as the means to success in all matters;
it is like the exceedingly great radiance of the sun.
It occurs for one who has indeed reached the middle of the sky. || 227 ||
Due to the inherent frailty of women, royal fortune, even when established in great power, does not remain like a harlot;
[just as she does not stay] upon the circle of the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa—
Even though it is fixed, the earth indeed trembles. || 228 ||
Fate alone is constant, whereas friendship and enmity are generally unstable; for by those very same people by whom one is favored...
With those very same dice, he wins again. || 229 ||
It is only through its infancy that this moon displays unevenness and crookedness;
yet when it is full of all its digits, [it shines with perfect symmetry].
Everyone becomes equal, like the moon. || 230 ||
Only the cunning among the deceitful perceive the hidden intentions of those of evil nature,
even when their speech is indirect.
Prostitutes do not understand this. || 231 ||
At present, virtues and those who recognize virtue are as difficult to find as prosperity; however,
faults are easily found along with the wicked.
In the Kali age, calamities abound like grass. || 232 ||
Due to the diversity of the accomplishment of tasks, even a lowly person may sometimes be sufficient, whereas a great man is never so;
it is just like a mirror made of bell-metal.
Even for kings, it is not made with gold. || 233 ||
Those who have not seen their own welfare do not acknowledge the virtues of the great, even though they exist;
by what means could they believe in greatness?
Well-frogs [do not know] the ocean.
Indeed, the very vices of the wicked bestow proficiency in evil deeds,
just as the poisons of serpents [bestow clarity] upon mirrors.
Anger inflames poison itself. || 235 ||
By their very faults, the wicked generally become manifest to the virtuous; just as people,
upon seeing a hare, [realize it is not a deer].
He cites the moon as an example of that which is possessed of a stain. || 236 ||
Even when broken like honey,
a virtuous person surely rejoins it through his own excellence;
but the wicked are like mallets.
They are proficient in analysis, not in synthesis. || 237 ||
Even knowledge produces a state of delusion for the wicked, just like ignorance;
it is like a torch that, despite illuminating, [causes distress].
It makes the birds blind to the light. || 238 ||
Even if the affection of a virtuous person should perish through fate, it nevertheless remains within sentient beings like the resonance of a bell.
Formative activity binds one for a long time. || 239 ||
Even those who are violent do not go to such an end as do the innocent through the faults of speech; by talkativeness, one becomes worse even than a crane.
The partridge indeed falls into misfortune. || 240 ||
Since the very same things that become great for the noble ones also lead to calamities,
they endure for a long time until the end of the age.
The sun alone consumes the world. || 241 ||
Even fortune, though naturally fickle,
attains stability through those of great being;
even mercury, though falling, [is stabilized] by means of alchemical processes.
Is that which belongs to another not bound? 242.
Having raised up the chaff, fools laboriously conceal the great wonder;
for what [wonder] has not surpassed the moon?
The clouds thicken only the darkness itself.
Though his words are sharp and conciliatory, this sweet yet deceitful man torments my heart excessively,
just as a sword whets its edge.
Likewise, even cold water is not fire. || 244 ||
When destruction has arrived, the activities of sentient beings become perverted;
even in a dream, one who is about to die does not [behave thus].
He sees the sun devoid of rays. || 245 ||
The great do not experience such distress in their own calamities as they do in the misfortunes of others;
they remain unshakable even when their own selves are struck down.
The earth trembles during the calamity of another. || 246 ||
For a wise person, it is not appropriate to place trust in the Lord, thinking "He is my kinsman" or "He is my friend," just as the wind cannot be trusted even by fire.
One who has risen destroys the flame of the lamp. || 247 ||
"This one has done me a favor; he is my friend"—the wicked have no such consideration for anyone.
[They abandon] their own refuge along with the Hotṛ priest.
A fire that has flared up consumes everything. || 248 ||
Everyone weighs what ought and ought not to be done when they are satisfied; one who is afflicted by thirst never does so, thinking only, "Is this water sweet or pure?"
Who traveling on the path through the sky reflects? || 249 ||
Making oneself excessively great,
one who has climbed to the top of a tree cannot remain there.
It neither remains nor does it arise. || 250 ||
Generally, the utterly dull-witted point to another as the cause of their own calamity, rather than themselves; yet both the object to be burned and the fire are [the cause].
Even so, burning arises by depending [on it]. || 251 ||
The conceit of those great in learning,
the pride of the wealthy, and the intoxication of the handsome are like the saltiness of the ocean's waters.
The wicked and evil sports of the God of Death. || 252 ||
"I am broad" and "this one is thinner; I am not accessible to him"—this is a lack of confidence.
For what is there in the fact that the head of a mountain is large?
The diamond cannot be split, even by a needle. || 253 ||
One who has not formed a firm conviction should be known as ignorant, like a blind man;
whereas for one whose intellect is settled, doubt is like that of one with clear vision regarding the nature of forms. This is generally the case.
Only those afflicted by cataracts [perceive them] as such. || 254 ||
Power overcomes even the exalted force of an enemy, for the body of one possessed of policy is not the deciding factor;
by means of it, one may pierce even a tiger.
How large is the tusk of the Boar? || 255 ||
For the virtuous, only good people serve as a refuge in times of distress, just as hands and feet do;
but the wicked are like hair and nails.
Only the transformations are employed. || 256 ||
Those who seize wealth entrusted to them,
even when guarded by skillful protectors, are recognized as fish that have been poorly caught.
Even while drinking water from lakes, they do not [drink it]. || 257 ||
Punishment is merely the majesty of the lord; for success, counsel alone is sufficient.
Austerity emaciates the body.
Wisdom alone purifies the mind. || 258 ||
Even though the scriptures of the Jina exist,
not everyone possesses skill in exposition;
one [person's] charm is different from another's.
The quality of discernment belongs to women. || 259 ||
Even without a cause, the wicked, intoxicated by the wine of their own faults, become reckless toward the virtuous;
for it is said that blood is beautiful here [only when flowing from them].
Thus do the Śabaras slay the Pāśupatas. || 260 ||
In some cases brilliance is praised,
but tranquility is commended in all circumstances by those who know the truth;
for fire hardens [the earth].
Water alone makes the clay soft. || 261 ||
He who, having obtained prosperity solely through giving, does not give again to those in need—
him one should not call ungrateful.
Objects of value attend upon him even more, as if out of anger [at his former neglect]. || 262 ||
He who desires to satisfy the ignorant with well-spoken words that follow the path of reason [must do so] from outside, through a door that has not been opened.
Surely he is splashing water.
A virtuous person, whose mind is intent on the welfare of others, does not undergo transformation even at the time of destruction;
like a sandalwood tree, even when being cut down.
The axe makes the mouth fragrant. || 264 ||
That speech which is not recited by virtuous people, not cultivated, not contemplated, and not desired to be spoken in an assembly—
such speech is so called only by name.
It is utterly displeasing, like the conduct of a pauper. || 265 ||
Perhaps someone, by merely observing this poem through familiarity,
might follow the path of the great ones.
Thus, this effort is even [directed toward] mere idle chatter. || 266 ||
Thus, while the sprouts of the virtues of auspicious seeds— wounded by the fire of the world’s manifold defects— are yet to emerge,
accumulate your fame before it is too late.
The thunderbolt-fall of death, the devourer of the three worlds. || 267 ||
By whom were the eyes of the female deer anointed? Who gathers the clusters of petals upon the lotuses?
And who creates the beautiful plumage of the peacocks?
For who indeed can bestow discipline upon those born of noble lineage? || 268 ||
*The Engagement in Worldly Convention*, a poetic work by Ācārya Ravigupta.
Appendix:
It is better indeed not to have formed an attachment at all.
But one whose love has been obstructed does not feel such pain;
for it is the one with eyes who suffers when they are clouded, not the one born blind.
Even a trifle leads to merit for the great, while even a great deed results in fault for the wicked;
even a blade of grass serves as milk for cows.
Even milk becomes poison for serpents.
Even in his final state, the wise man does not abandon his own quality due to the purity of his birth;
he does not relinquish his whiteness.
A conch shell, even when worn and then released by a peacock, [remains pure]. || 3.271 ||
A wicked person, rejoicing in the misfortunes of others, does not even consider his own destruction,
especially when a thousand others are perishing.
A headless torso dances at the front of the battle.
An unmanageable servant, deceitful friends, a stingy master,
and a wife devoid of discipline.
There are four types of headaches. || 5 = 273 ||
A maiden [despises] one who lacks resolve, is lazy, relies solely on fate, and is devoid of human effort, just as she would a husband who is aged.
Lakṣmī does not wish to embrace him.
Even when facing his own destruction,
a wicked person does not reckon the suffering caused by another's misfortune; for generally, when a thousand perish, he remains unmoved.
A headless torso dances at the front of the battle.
By a chance occurrence, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow,
Fortune momentarily bestows her favor upon one who lacks self-control.
That is her feminine fickleness.
Like a cluster of blossoms,
there are only two courses for a high-minded person:
either to stand at the head of all the world, or to wither away.
Or he may perish right there in the forest.
In some particular case,
even a defect attains equality with a virtue; for indeed, a fracture itself becomes an ornament.
It occurs in the lower jewel of women. || 10 = 278 ||
A good person brings about renown;
a skilled poet merely composes poetry;
water nourishes the lotus.
But the Sun appoints one to prosperity. || 11 = 279 ||

Without having studied this [Prajñāpāramitā]— which is profound, clear in its entirety, possesses a few sūtras, has infinite gateways, and is the seal of the syllables— how could one [attain liberation]?
He drifts upon the ocean of debate. || 12 = 280 ||
"I am virtuous; what foreign land could be like mine?"— this mere fragment of false pride shines only upon the eyes when applied as collyrium.
It is not placed again on the lower jewel. || 12a = 281 ||
Even one who is like the Omniscient One in his virtues perishes when alone and without support; even a priceless ruby [is lost]...
It depends upon its own substratum. || 13 = 282 ||
The jewel of the mind, when unafflicted, is called internal wealth;
for one by whom it is corrupted by defects, [that wealth is lost].
For him, all calamities [arise]. || 14 = 283 ||

These rays of his, which act as a miraculous collyrium that dispels the darkness from the rows of eyes of the world, render the three worlds fruitful; oh, consider this— that for embodied beings, there is indeed some karma that cannot be transgressed!
That jewel of the sky has rays that cause blindness for owls. || 15 = 284 ||
One who has not committed sin abandons fear;
learning abandons the deceitful and the negligent;
modesty abandons the lustful; and prosperity abandons the lazy.
The world [regards] a woman as cruel and wicked. || 16 = 285 ||
The skillful attains prosperity; one who eats wholesome food attains health and happiness; the disease-free person attains well-being; and the industrious person reaches the end of knowledge.
And one who is disciplined attains virtue, wealth, and fame. || 17 = 286 ||
For those possessed of virtues, even a great fault becomes a virtue; for those possessed of faults, even a good deed becomes a fault;
and for cows, even a blade of grass serves as milk.
Even milk is poison for serpents.
The Lord of Destiny is sovereign not only over humans, but even over the gods, as long as there is a friend who is the master of wealth.
Hara is clothed in skin. || 19 = 288 ||
The anger of virtuous men does not arise, or if it arises, it does not last long; and even if it lasts long, it does not prove false.
He is equal to the low-born in affection. || 20 = 289 ||
"O mother devoted to dharma, show compassion for me, who am weary and a stranger; I shall go quietly to the corner of the porch by the door and sleep there during the night.
Having said this, he was suddenly rebuked by the words of his fierce wife.
The traveler, his wealth consisting of a handful of straw tucked under his arm, has set out once more. || 21 = 290 ||
Garlic, though perfumed with the scents of musk, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood,
does not relinquish its foul odor.
A base person [clings] to his nature as if it were born together with him. || 22 = 291 ||
For even when his rise has begun,
a wicked person first spreads distress among his own kin, just as a forest fire spreading while ascending causes heat.
The wood burns its own place of birth. || 23 = 292 ||
Even for the wicked who dwell together,
there is no intimacy, just as between a lotus and water; whereas for the virtuous, even when dwelling far apart, there is union.
Joy becomes like the moon upon the night-lotus. || 24 = 293 ||
